copy.project_title: Testing Evidence and Authorization Checks for Tool-Using Agents

live_form_copy.applicant_or_team_under_200_words: I am Christopher Ongko, a master's researcher at Yuan Ze University. I built Hardware-Splicer, an open, versioned environment for studying how tool-using AI agents make hardware-engineering decisions when evidence is partial, contradictory, or tied to the wrong revision. The system separates model reasoning from deterministic checks, project state, source provenance, and human approval. My background combines finance and accounting research with hands-on development of agentic hardware systems and research infrastructure. I will conduct the proposed study as a small independent university-affiliated project. I will not claim faculty, laboratory, or institutional sponsorship unless it is formally established.
live_form_copy.research_and_credit_request_under_300_wo: I propose a matched-condition study of a narrow safety question: when a tool-using AI agent has a plausible plan but incomplete, stale, or contradictory evidence, can checks outside the model reduce unsupported action attempts without blocking useful work? Hardware-Splicer provides the test environment. It separately tracks component identity, source evidence, project revision, deterministic engineering constraints, and human approval. I will evaluate Claude on a frozen ten-case corpus containing partial evidence, identity conflicts, tool failures, a plausible but wrong analogy, and stale revision evidence. The same cases will run in a reference tool-using condition and with Hardware-Splicer checks enabled. Consequential reference actions remain advisory or dry-run; the study does not require unsafe physical execution. The core design uses 200 Claude Sonnet 5 runs and 100 Claude Opus 5 confirmatory runs. Outcomes include unsupported actions, correct abstention, false blocking, task completion, human intervention, stale-state carryover, and recovery after evidence or tool failure. Free API credits are important because I am conducting this as a small university-affiliated project without a dedicated model-evaluation budget. Credits would make repeated matched runs possible instead of relying on a few demonstrations. Planned outputs are a reproducible protocol, case-level failure taxonomy, quantitative analysis, versioned traces where policy permits, and a technical report or paper draft.

copy.research_summary:
I am interested in a narrow safety question that comes up once an AI agent can call tools: what should happen when the model has a plausible plan but the evidence behind it is incomplete, stale, or contradictory?

I will study this using Hardware-Splicer, a hardware-engineering environment I built where the model can inspect evidence, plan work, and use tools, but several decisions remain outside the model. The system separately tracks component identity, project revision, deterministic engineering checks, and human approval. Hardware is useful here because a weakly supported answer can have an obvious downstream consequence, while the experiment can still keep the reference condition in advisory/dry-run mode.

Claude will be evaluated on a frozen ten-case corpus that includes partial evidence, identity conflict, parser/tool failure, a plausible but wrong analogy, and stale revision evidence. I will compare a reference tool-using condition with the same tasks when the external checks are enabled.

The main outcomes are unsupported action attempts, correct abstention, false blocking, useful task completion, human intervention, stale-state carryover, and recovery after evidence or tool failure. The core design uses 200 Claude Sonnet 5 runs and 100 Claude Opus 5 confirmatory runs. The goal is not to claim a general solution to alignment; it is to test whether a specific control design helps an agent stop at the right boundary without making it unable to do useful work.
copy.why_ai_safety:
The safety claim I want to test is deliberately small. When the model says something that the surrounding evidence does not support, does the system prevent that assertion from escalating into an action? And when the evidence is sufficient, can the agent still complete the task without unnecessary blocking?

The experiment therefore looks at unsupported assertions that move toward action, whether missing or conflicting evidence causes appropriate abstention, whether a revision change invalidates stale state, whether deterministic checks provide a useful control layer outside the model, how the agent recovers after tool or evidence failures, and how much useful task completion is lost, if any, when those checks are present.

Hardware is the test environment, not the funding objective. The object of study is tool-using agent behavior under explicit control and review mechanisms.
planned_use_of_claude: Claude Sonnet 5 primary: 10 cases × 2 conditions × 10 repeats = 200 scored runs.
Claude Opus 5 confirmatory: 10 cases × 2 conditions × 5 repeats = 100 scored runs.
Small unscored pilot before freezing transport/token assumptions.
Same frozen corpus, evaluator, protocol, and adjudication rules across conditions.
Preserve tool calls, revision state, outcome labels, failures, retries, and usage metadata where policy permits.
copy.exploratory_model_policy: Claude Fable 5.1 is not part of the preregistered core. It may be added later only as a separately declared exploratory run if the core results justify it and the then-current retention/cost terms are acceptable.

expected_outputs: Quantitative summaries of unsupported actions, abstention, false blocking, completion, intervention, stale-state carryover, and recovery.

copy.strongest_one_sentence_contribution: The study asks whether simple checks outside the model can stop weakly supported agent decisions from turning into actions while still leaving the agent useful.
nonclaims: Do not claim Hardware-Splicer is a general alignment solution.
Do not claim Claude has already passed the benchmark.
Do not claim the experiment proves universal agent safety.
